'''''Verbena bonariensis''''', commonly known as the '''purpletop vervain''', '''clustertop vervain''', '''Argentinian vervain''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref> '''tall verbena''' or '''pretty verbena''', is a member of the [[Verbenaceae|verbena]] [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] cultivated as a flowering annual or [[herbaceous plant|herbaceous]] [[perennial plant]]. In United States horticulture, it is also known by the ambiguous names '''[[purpletop]]''' (also used for the grass ''[[Tridens flavus]]'') and '''South American vervain''' (which can mean any of the numerous [[species]] in the [[genus]] ''[[Verbena]]'' occurring on the continent). For the misapplication "Brazilian verbena", see [[#Taxonomy and systematics|below]].

It is [[native plant|native]] to [[tropics|tropical]] South America where it grows throughout most of the warm regions, from Colombia and Brazil to Argentina and Chile.

==Description==
''Verbena bonariensis'' is a tall and slender-stemmed perennial. It can grow to {{cvt|6|ft}} tall and can spread to {{cvt|3|ft}} wide. At maturity, it will develop a woody base. Fragrant lavender to rose-purple flowers are in tight clusters located on terminal and axillary stems, blooming from mid-summer until fall frost. The stem is square with very long internodes. Leaves are ovate to ovate-lanceolate with a toothed margin and grow up to {{cvt|4|in}} long.

==Etymology==
''Verbena'' is derived from [[Latin]], meaning ‘sacred bough’, in reference to the leafy twigs of vervaine (''[[Verbena officinalis]]'') which were historically carried by priests, used in wreaths for druidic rituals, and for medicine. Named by Virgil and [[Pliny the Elder]]. The common name, vervaine, comes from the [[Celtic languages|Celtic]] name, ‘ferfain’.<ref name="gledhill">Gledhill, David (2008). "The Names of Plants". Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|9780521866453}} (hardback), {{ISBN|9780521685535}} (paperback). pp 74, 399</ref>

Its [[specific name (botany)|specific epithet]] ''bonariensis'' means 'from [[Buenos Aires]], [[Argentina]]'. ''Buenos'' means 'good' and ''aires'' means 'air' ('good air').<ref name="gledhill"/><ref>[http://www.calflora.net/botanicalnames/pageBL-BY.html CalFlora Botanical Names]</ref> All together, its name translates to "The sacred bough from the land of good air".

==Taxonomy and systematics==
 <!--(...where the [[Biological type|type specimen]] probably was received from) reliable information on specimen origins was sometimes hard to get in Linnaeus' time, and it may be that he simply conjectured the island of Bonaire to be the place of origin. In any case, the actual collection localities of overseas type specimen are rarely given in 18th-century sources; rather, the point of shipment is normally used if a specific locality is used at all. - Comment from Franz Xaver: In his diagnosis Linnaeus cites Dillenius (Hortus Elthamenis) "Verbena bonariensis altissima, lavandulae canariensis folio, spica lavendulae". Obviously this is the source where the name comes from. Linnaeus adds "Habitat in agro Bonariensi" for the location of origin. "Ager Bonariensis" means "Field or land of B." This more likely refers to the Pampas around Buenos Aires than to Bonaire. -->

''Verbena bonariensis'' is a member of the South American vervains, which are [[polyploidy|polyploid]] and have more than 14 [[chromosome]]s. Among these, it is part of a lineage which might also include ''[[Verbena intermedia]]'' and seems well distant from ''[[Verbena litoralis]]'' or ''[[Verbena montevidensis]]'' for example.<ref>Yuan & Olmstead (2008)</ref>

Sometimes, the name ''[[Verbena brasiliensis]]'', Brazilian verbena or Brazilian vervain, is found for this species.<ref>E.g. USDA (2007)</ref> However, this is the result of a mix-up with ''V. brasiliensis'', the "true" Brazilian verbena, which has been erroneously referred to as ''V. bonariaensis'' by several botanists.<ref>UDSA (2008a)</ref>

There are two named [[subspecies]]:<ref>ITIS [2000]</ref>{{Citation needed|date=August 2008}}<!-- need a reference to describe differences -->

* ''Verbena bonariensis'' subsp. ''conglomerata'' <small>Briq.</small>

==Cultivation==
[[File:Bonariensis.jpg|thumb]]
''V. bonariensis'' is cultivated as an [[ornamental plant]] for traditional and [[xeriscape|drought tolerant]] and 'pollinator-host' gardens and parks.

It is a perennial, hardy in [[Hardiness zone|USDA Zones]] 7-11. It can be grown as an annual in areas where it is not winter hardy and will bloom in the first year when grown from seed. Its long internodes give it a sparse appearance but allow it to intermingle and coexist with other plants. The flowers, which appear in mid- to late summer, are very attractive to butterflies, and provide nectar for native bees and many beneficial garden insects.

This species grows best in a well-drained soil. It prefers full sun to partial shade and needs regular moisture. It has a reputation of rarely being attacked by insect pests, but may be susceptible to [[powdery mildew]]. ''V. bonariensis'' is commonly grown from seed which germinates readily without pre-treatment, but can also be [[Plant propagation|propagated]] from herbaceous stem [[Cuttings (plant)|cuttings]].

It has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Verbena bonariensis'' | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/42079/verbena-bonariensis/details|access-date=21 August 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 106 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 5 February 2019}}</ref>

==Invasive species==
''V. bonariensis'' self-seeds readily. This ability has raised concerns that it may become an [[invasive species]] and [[noxious weed]] in favorable [[habitat]]s.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.cal-ipc.org/plants/risk/verbena-bonariensis-risk/|title=Verbena bonariensis Risk|date=2017-10-15|work=California Invasive Plant Council|access-date=2020-03-16|language=en-US}}</ref> It has naturalized in a number of southern United States.

Presently, the plant is on the [[invasive species]] watchlist for [[Washington (state)|Washington state]],<ref>WSNWCB (2007)</ref> naturalized in tropical and southern Africa, temperate Asia, Australia, New Zealand, the United States (including [[Hawaii]]), the [[West Indies]], [[Macaronesia]] and the [[Mascarene Islands]]. According to [[Pacific Island Ecosystems at Risk]], it is considered a weed in [[Fiji]], [[New Guinea]] and other [[South Pacific islands]].<ref>[http://www.hear.org/pier/species/verbena_bonariensis.htm Pacific Island Ecosystems at Risk: ''V. bonariensis'']</ref>
